message:
QUESTION:
How much did the average-speed cameras reduce injury collisions at the 10 sites, and what would a city-wide rollout achieve?

DATA:
Average-speed cameras at 10 sites, installed January 2023. The 10 sites were chosen because they had the highest numbers of injury collisions in the city in 2020-2022.

| | 2020-2022 (3 years before) | 2023-2025 (3 years after) |
| Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites | 156 | 102 |
| Injury collisions on all other city roads | 3,600 | 3,240 |

Traffic: a bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Traffic counts at the 10 sites fell by an average of 15% between the two periods. Traffic on other city roads was broadly unchanged.

Speed surveys at the camera sites (speed limit 30 mph): mean speed 34 mph before installation, 31 mph after.

The 10 sites are all urban arterial roads. The city has about 900 km of roads, of which the camera sites cover about 12 km. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts.

<analysis>
# Average-speed cameras: three-year evaluation

## Summary

Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites fell by 35%, from 156 to 102. This overstates what the cameras achieved. After allowing for the city-wide trend, the fall is about 27%, or roughly 13 collisions a year. Two other factors would have reduced collisions at these sites without cameras:

- **Regression to the mean.** The sites were chosen because they had the most collisions in 2020-2022.
- **A new bypass.** It took through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites and cut traffic at the sites by 15% on average.

After also allowing for traffic volume, the estimate falls to about 15%, or around 6 collisions a year. At these collision counts, that figure is **not statistically distinguishable from no effect**. Its 95% interval runs from about a one-third reduction to a 10% increase. Correcting for regression to the mean would probably lower the estimate further, by an amount we can't yet measure.

**The collision data alone cannot confirm that the cameras worked.** The main evidence for a real effect is the speed data. Mean speeds fell by 3 mph. Established speed-collision models suggest a fall that size would reduce injury collisions by roughly 10-20%. So the cameras probably did reduce collisions at these sites, but by an uncertain and possibly modest amount.

These results do not support a city-wide figure. Most of the network is residential streets, which are unlike the arterial roads studied here.

## Background

Average-speed cameras were installed at 10 sites in January 2023. All 10 are urban arterial roads. Together they cover about 12 km of the city's 900 km network, or about 1.3%. This note compares injury collisions in the three full years before installation (2020-2022) with the three full years after (2023-2025). It does so at the 10 sites and on all other city roads.¹

## Raw change

| | 2020-2022 | 2023-2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Camera sites | 156 (52/yr) | 102 (34/yr) | −35% |
| All other roads | 3,600 (1,200/yr) | 3,240 (1,080/yr) | −10% |

The raw fall at the sites is 54 collisions over three years. With counts this small, chance alone gives a 95% interval on the before/after ratio of about 0.51-0.84. The raw fall is therefore unlikely to be pure noise, but its size is imprecise. Most of it may also come from causes other than the cameras, as set out below.

## Allowing for the background trend

Collisions fell 10% on other roads. If the sites had followed that trend, we would have expected 46.8 collisions a year, against 34 observed. That is about 13 fewer a year, a relative reduction of about 27% (0.654 ÷ 0.900 = 0.727). The 95% interval on this ratio is roughly 0.56-0.94, which still excludes "no effect".

This assumes the sites would otherwise have behaved like the rest of the network. Several things make that unlikely.

## Factors that bias the estimate

**1. Regression to the mean (inflates the apparent effect).** The sites were selected because they had the city's highest collision counts in 2020-2022. Part of any site's high count in a given period is random bad luck. Sites picked for a high count will therefore tend to record fewer collisions in the next period, whatever is done to them. So the 2020-2022 baseline overstates the sites' typical collision rate, and the before/after comparison overstates the reduction.

In road-safety evaluations this effect is often large, sometimes accounting for a substantial share of the apparent benefit at hotspot sites. We cannot size it here without collision data from before 2020, or a comparison group of similar high-collision sites that did not get cameras.

**2. The bypass and lower traffic (inflates the apparent effect).** The bypass opened in March 2023. It diverted through-traffic from 6 of the 10 sites, and traffic at the sites fell 15% on average. Traffic elsewhere was broadly unchanged.

Fewer vehicles means fewer collisions. As a rough adjustment, suppose collisions scale in proportion to traffic. Then the expected count without cameras becomes 46.8 × 0.85 ≈ 39.8 a year, against 34 observed. That is about 6 fewer collisions a year, a reduction of about 15%. The 95% interval on this ratio is roughly 0.66-1.10, which includes no effect.

This adjustment may over-correct. Studies of traffic flow and collisions often find that collisions rise less than proportionally with traffic, so a 15% fall in traffic may cut collisions by less than 15%. The 15% figure should therefore not be read as a floor. Before any correction for regression to the mean, the true figure could lie somewhere between 15% and 27%. The bypass may also have changed speeds or the mix of traffic at the 6 affected sites, which this simple adjustment ignores.

**3. Contamination of the comparison group (inflates the apparent effect).** "All other city roads" may not be a clean control, for two reasons:

- **The bypass itself.** If the bypass lies within the city and its collisions are counted in the 2023-2025 total of 3,240, the background decline on pre-existing roads is understated.
- **Displacement.** Drivers avoiding the camera routes would add traffic, and possibly collisions, to nearby roads.

Both would make the background trend look weaker than it was, and so make the camera effect look larger. We should check whether the bypass is included in the 3,240.

**Note on the intervals.** All the intervals above reflect only the random variation in collision counts. They do not include uncertainty in the adjustments themselves, or extra site-to-site variation beyond pure chance. The true uncertainty is therefore wider.

## Speed evidence

Mean speeds at the camera sites fell from 34 mph to 31 mph. That is a drop of 3 mph, or about 9%, and the mean is still slightly above the 30 mph limit.

Lower speeds reduce both the chance of a collision and its severity. Under Nilsson's power model, injury collisions scale with roughly the square of the speed ratio. Here (31/34)² ≈ 0.83, which implies about a 17% reduction. Elvik's later re-estimates suggest lower exponents for urban roads, of roughly 1-1.5, which imply a 9-13% reduction. Taken together, a fall of this size plausibly reduces injury collisions by **roughly 10-20%**. This range is independent of the collision counts and broadly consistent with the 15% traffic-adjusted figure.

This is the main reason to think the cameras had a genuine effect. There is one caveat. The bypass may also have changed speeds at 6 of the sites, so not all of the speed fall can be credited to the cameras. If regression to the mean turns out to explain much of the collision fall, the speed evidence becomes correspondingly more important. In that case, separating the cameras' and the bypass's contributions to the speed change matters more.

## What can be concluded

| Adjustment | Collisions prevented per year | Reduction | Approx. 95% interval on ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| None (raw) | 18 | 35% | 0.51-0.84 |
| Background trend | ~13 | ~27% | 0.56-0.94 |
| Trend + traffic volume | ~6 | ~15% | 0.66-1.10 |
| + regression to the mean | Lower, size unknown | Unknown | — |

The cameras probably reduced injury collisions at these sites. That conclusion rests mainly on the 3 mph speed drop, not on the collision counts. After adjusting for traffic, the counts alone cannot rule out no effect. The true effect is likely well below the 27% trend-adjusted figure. The speed evidence points to something in the region of 10-20%, possibly less once regression to the mean is accounted for.

## City-wide rollout

The 27% figure cannot be applied to the whole network, for three reasons:

- **It is not a reliable estimate of the effect even at the 10 sites.** See the adjustments above.
- **The sites are not representative.** They are high-collision arterial roads where speeds were above the limit. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts and, probably, lower speeds. A camera can only prevent collisions that would otherwise have happened. On a street with few collisions and little speeding, the absolute benefit would be small.
- **The network-wide figure assumes cameras everywhere.** Multiplying 27% by the roughly 1,080 annual collisions on other roads gives about 290 a year. That would require cameras across the whole network. Most of those collisions are spread thinly across streets where average-speed cameras would be neither practical nor cost-effective.

A rollout to further high-collision arterial roads is more defensible than a city-wide one. Its likely benefit should be estimated from a corrected effect size and the specific candidate sites.

## Recommendations

1. **Do not fund a city-wide programme on the basis of this evaluation.**
2. **Re-estimate the effect properly.** Obtain site-level and monthly data, and:
   - Use collision data from before 2020, or an empirical Bayes method, to correct for regression to the mean.
   - Find a comparison group of similar high-collision arterial roads without cameras.
   - Check whether bypass collisions are included in the "other roads" total, and look for displacement onto roads near the camera sites.
   - Compare the 4 sites unaffected by the bypass with the 6 affected sites. At roughly 15 and 20 collisions a year respectively, this will be very imprecise and should be treated as indicative only. Speed data at the 4 unaffected sites will be especially useful, because it isolates the cameras' effect on speed from the bypass.
   - Report killed or seriously injured (KSI) collisions separately, if available. Speed reductions mainly reduce severity, so this is where a camera effect is most likely to show.
3. **If the corrected effect is still worthwhile,** consider extending cameras to the next-highest-collision arterial roads. Use a full business case that sets installation, maintenance and enforcement costs against the value of collisions prevented.
4. **Continue annual monitoring** at the original 10 sites, including speed surveys.
5. **Publish the evaluation,** including its limitations, so residents can see the results.

---

¹ The cameras operated for about two months (January-February 2023) before the bypass opened. If monthly data are available, that period could be examined separately, although it is too short to give a precise estimate on its own.
</analysis>

<review>
# Review of the average-speed camera evaluation

This is a strong analysis. It identifies the main threats to validity (regression to the mean, the bypass, comparison-group contamination). It quantifies uncertainty, triangulates with the speed data, and declines to give a city-wide figure that the data can't support. I re-checked all the arithmetic and intervals, and they hold. My suggestions are mostly additions and a few refinements.

## Arithmetic check

| Claim | Check | OK? |
|---|---|---|
| Raw −35%, 95% CI 0.51–0.84 | 102/156 = 0.654; SE(log) = √(1/156 + 1/102) = 0.127 → 0.510–0.839 | ✓ |
| Trend-adjusted 0.727, CI 0.56–0.94 | 0.654/0.900; adding 1/3600 + 1/3240 gives SE 0.130 → 0.564–0.937 | ✓ |
| Expected 46.8/yr, ~13 fewer | 52 × 0.9 = 46.8; 46.8 − 34 = 12.8 | ✓ |
| Traffic-adjusted ~15%, CI 0.66–1.10 | 34/39.78 = 0.855 → 0.663–1.102; ~5.8 fewer per year | ✓ |
| Power model, exponent 2 | (31/34)² = 0.831 → 17% | ✓ |
| Exponent 1–1.5 | 0.912 and 0.871 → 9–13% | ✓ |
| City-wide naive figure | 0.27 × 1,080 ≈ 292 | ✓ |

## Substantive issues

**1. The 2020–2022 baseline includes the COVID period (not mentioned).**
This is the most important omission. 2020, and parts of 2021, had unusual traffic volumes and patterns. The trend adjustment only removes this if arterial roads and the mainly residential "other roads" were affected in the same way. That is doubtful: commuting and through-traffic changed differently from local trips, and some places saw higher speeds on emptier arterials. The sites were also selected on counts from this unusual period. At minimum, the analysis should flag this as another reason the comparison group may be a poor counterfactual. If annual data exist, it could check whether 2020 is anomalous at the sites relative to other roads.

**2. The bypass could push speeds either way.**
The speed section implies the bypass may account for some of the 3 mph drop, so the cameras deserve less credit. But lower traffic volumes usually *raise* free-flow speeds. Removing through-traffic could lower or raise mean speeds depending on how fast that traffic was moving. The direction is ambiguous, and the bypass may even have masked part of the camera effect. I'd reword this to say the bypass could bias the speed comparison in either direction. That also strengthens the case for the 4-versus-6 site comparison.

**3. The "roughly 15 and 20 collisions a year" split is unsupported.**
No site-level data are given. These figures appear to be 4/10 and 6/10 of the *after*-period rate of 34/yr, which assumes collisions are spread evenly across sites. Based on the before period, the split would be about 21 and 31. Either state the assumption or drop the numbers and just say the subgroups will be small.

**4. The traffic adjustment uses an unweighted average.**
The 15% fall is an average across sites. If only 6 sites lost traffic, those sites fell by roughly 25%, and the right adjustment depends on how collisions are distributed between the two groups. It's worth a sentence, and it is another reason to get site-level data.

## Smaller points

- **Answer the city-wide question directly.** The summary's last line could state that the data cannot support a city-wide figure. The naive extrapolation (~290 a year) would need cameras on every street and assumes an effect size that isn't established. Readers who asked for a number should see why none is given.
- **Regression to the mean.** "We cannot size it here" is right for the data in hand. The recommendations could add that an empirical Bayes correction needs a model fitted to comparable arterial roads, not just more years of data at these 10 sites.
- **Speed range rounding.** The body computes 9–17%, and the summary rounds this to 10–20%. That's fine, but "roughly 10–17%" would match the body more closely.
- **Recommendation 1** is appropriately firm, given the 95% interval includes no effect.

## Verdict

The analysis is sound and well-hedged, and its conclusions follow from the evidence. Adding the COVID-baseline caveat and correcting the bypass-speed reasoning would close the main gaps. The other points are minor clarifications.
</review>
